THE SPIRIT'S REFUSAL AS EVIDENCE. 'admitting that his own spirit could not accommodate itself to the text.' The composition reports a reader's response as a ground of standing; Secondary Source records it as the preface's own operation, with no reading of motive.

THE LATER EDITIONS. The 1530 preface is the replacement Secondary Source names (stratum 3.6); '1534' is the year of the complete Bible, and whether its preface differs from 1530 is not checked here.

AGAINST THE PREDICTION. Placed last: borne out ('at the back'). Standing disputed: borne out ('disputed antilegomena'). The figure deciding the standing: borne out, as the measure ('failed to clearly teach Christ'). Date: not addressed.

SMALLEST REPAIR. 'In 1522 Luther set Hebrews, James, Jude and Revelation at the end of his New Testament without numbers, and judged Revelation by whether it taught Christ as he found Christ taught in the gospels and Paul; in 1530 he wrote a new preface reading it as a history of the church.' [QUERENT] luther preface to revelation 1522

[SYSTEM] AI Overview
In his 1522 Preface to Revelation, Martin Luther expressed deep skepticism toward the Book of Revelation, placing it among the disputed antilegomena at the back of his New Testament. He famously doubted its apostolic or prophetic origins, complained that it failed to clearly teach Christ, and struggled with its cryptic and overwhelming imagery, admitting that his own spirit could not accommodate itself to the text. Luther's view softened in later editions, such as his 1530 and 1534 revisions, where he reinterpreted the book more favorably as a symbolic depiction of the church's spiritual struggle.
Bible Research +4
